verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 3 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.3; Kale 1902 and Wortham 1886 no. 3; Ramachandra Budhendra's southern text no. 2; Kosambi critical ed. no. 8, Group I = best-attested)
attribution_note: Kosambi places it in Group I (found in essentially all versions), so it is among the most securely Bhartrihari verses. Our ref_label gives no Kosambi number; it is K8.
translation_note: Accurate. 'durvidagdha' is glossed 'arrogant' by Telang's commentator and 'one who fancies himself a pandit' by Ramachandra Budhendra; 'puffed up' captures both. The line's 'God' stands for Brahma, the creator.
context: The opening verse of the section on fools (murkha-paddhati), right after the poet's complaint that the learned are jealous, the powerful proud and the rest ignorant. Ramachandra Budhendra introduces it as the answer to 'what kind of person is the fool?': not the ignorant, but the half-learned. The next verses list impossible feats that are still easier than pleasing such a mind.

key_terms.sense: one who does not know; the plainly ignorant, open to instruction
one who knows the fine distinctions; the real expert
spoiled or made conceited by a mere scrap (lava) of knowledge

core_teaching: The ignorant can be taught and the expert can be reasoned with, but a person proud of a little learning is closed to everyone. The real 'fool' of this section is the half-learned, conceited mind.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: The ignorant are set right by mere instruction; the true expert grasps distinctions at once; but one who thinks himself a pandit on a scrap of learning cannot be settled by any words. He is the real fool.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Heads the verse 'half knowledge causes trouble': the simple and the truly learned are easy to bring round, but one who struts on a little knowledge cannot be pleased even by Brahma, let alone by people.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang (1874/1893 edition: notes citing two Sanskrit commentaries, one by Ramarshi)
commentaries.gist: The commentator explains durvidagdha as 'arrogant'; Ramarshi as 'imperfectly educated'. Telang compares the English saying that a little learning is a dangerous thing.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Compares St Paul (1 Corinthians 8:2: whoever thinks he knows something does not yet know as he ought) and Pope's 'a little learning is a dangerous thing'.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a mirror before a verdict: the hardest person to teach is the one who has learned just enough to stop listening, and that can be any of us after a first success, a course or a few articles.
misreadings: Not a licence to label people who disagree with you as half-learned; commentators place the danger in the conceit, which the reader should check in themself first.
Not contempt for beginners or the unschooled: the verse says the ignorant are easy to teach.
cautions: Satire. Read flat it can sound arrogant; frame it as self-examination.
speaks_to: frustration at arguing with someone who will not listen
noticing one's own know-it-all phase
students and new professionals after early success
managers dealing with confident but shallow expertise
not_for: someone already feeling stupid or 'not enough'
a reader in a painful family conflict who might use it to write off a relative
research_note: No classical bhashya; commentators used are Ramachandra Budhendra's Sanskrit tika, Pandey's modern Sanskrit-Hindi commentary, and the notes of Telang, Kale and Wortham.

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 4 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.4; Kale and Wortham no. 4; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 3; Kosambi no. 9, Group I)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 9 confirmed (Group I).
translation_note: Accurate. Small point: 'santaret' is 'cross', not specifically 'swim'; Ramachandra Budhendra imagines crossing by some boat or other means. 'maṇi' may be a gem or pearl (Wortham cites the fable of pearls between crocodiles' teeth).
context: Second verse of the section on fools. Ramachandra Budhendra says that in two verses (this and the next, on oil from sand and water from a mirage) the poet shows how hard it is to win the obstinate fool's mind. It follows the verse on the half-learned (Niti 3).

key_terms.sense: the fangs in a crocodile's (or sea monster's) mouth
dug in, obstinately set in a contrary view
one could win over, please, bring round

core_teaching: Feats that look impossible can be managed with some method, but there is no method for winning over a mind that has dug in against you. Effort spent there is wasted.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Each danger named can be overcome by some means: a trick, a boat, a charm against snakes. For the fool possessed by stubbornness (durāgraha) there is no means at all, so his mind cannot be won.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Reads the closing optative as advice: one may brave crocodile, sea and snake, but should not even try to please the obstinate fool's mind.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang (1874/1893 edition: notes citing two Sanskrit commentaries, one by Ramarshi)
commentaries.gist: Glosses pratiniviṣṭa as perverse, headstrong in holding a contrary opinion.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Explains the image by the old fable that crocodiles carry pearls between their teeth.

practical_reading: Used as permission to stop: when someone has made up their mind against you, more argument rarely helps; save your energy for what can move.
misreadings: Not a claim that people never change; the target is the dug-in posture (pratiniveśa), not the person's whole future.
Not advice to write off family or colleagues after one disagreement.
cautions: Can harden contempt for a specific person; pair with Niti 3 and 8, which turn the same lens on oneself.
speaks_to: exhaustion from repeated arguments
deciding when to stop trying to convince someone
workplace or family stalemates
not_for: someone grieving an estrangement who may hear it as 'they will never change'
a reader looking for reasons to cut off help-seeking

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 8 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.8, reading 'dvipa iva' for 'gaja iva'; Kale and Wortham no. 8; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 7; Kosambi no. 5, Group I)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 5 confirmed (Group I). Ramachandra Budhendra frames it as 'an experienced person telling others what happened to him', so the 'I' need not be autobiographical.
translation_note: Accurate. 'mada' carries a double sense, elephant's rut and human vanity, as Kale notes.
context: In the section on fools, after verses on the impossibility of pleasing the conceited, the speaker turns the charge on himself: he too was blind with pride when he knew a little. The cure was learning, bit by bit, in the presence of the wise.

key_terms.sense: blinded by mada: rut in an elephant, intoxicating pride in a person
from being near the learned; in their company

core_teaching: Pride grows from knowing a little; real contact with deeper knowledge shows how much one does not know, and that recognition dissolves pride as a fever breaks.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Cites the maxim 'little learning, great pride' and the Upanishadic idea that one who has a teacher truly knows. Whoever knowing little thinks himself all-knowing is the fool; whoever knowing much counts himself a fool is wise.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Plain sense: with a little knowledge I strutted like a rutting elephant; once I began learning from scholars I saw I was a fool, and the pride left like a fever.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Notes the double meaning of mada (rut and vanity) and disagrees with Telang's reading: people are puffed up by little knowledge, not great.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Reports Telang's view that 'knowing a little' is the speaker's later judgment: when I knew what I now see was only a little.

practical_reading: A model of honest self-correction: the sign that you are learning is that you feel less certain; seek out people who know more than you and let them deflate you.
misreadings: Not a call to self-contempt; 'I am a fool' is the healthy recognition that ends arrogance, not a verdict on one's worth.
cautions: Readers with low self-esteem may hear 'I am a fool' literally; emphasise the relief of the fever breaking.
speaks_to: embarrassment over past arrogance
students moving from beginner confidence to real study
anyone humbled by a mentor or a new field
early-career overconfidence
not_for: someone in acute shame or self-criticism
a reader who already feels stupid

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 14 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.14; Kale and Wortham no. 14; not in Ramachandra Budhendra's southern text; Kosambi no. 320, Group II)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 320 confirmed. It is Group II, a verse Kosambi marks as attested in more than one version but one 'there is reason to suspect'. It is missing from Ramachandra Budhendra's southern recension. Fine to cite as from the Nitishataka; avoid claiming it as certainly Bhartrihari's own.
translation_note: 'vanacara' can mean forest-dwelling people (Kale 'foresters'; Pandey glosses forest tribes) or wild animals (Wortham). Our 'creatures of the forest' and the line's 'animals' are a defensible choice and avoid an unhappy contrast with tribal people.
context: Closes the section on fools in the Chaukhamba and Kale ordering, after verses on people without learning being beasts in human form. It sums up the section's advice: avoid company with the closed and foolish, whatever the comfort on offer.

key_terms.sense: forest-goer: forest dwellers or wild animals
close contact, keeping company, with fools
the palace of Indra, king of the gods

core_teaching: The company you keep matters more than the comfort of your surroundings; hardship among the simple is better than luxury among fools.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Living with forest folk in rough terrain is somehow bearable, but living with great fools is to be shunned even if it came with a royal palace or heaven.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang (1874/1893 edition: notes citing two Sanskrit commentaries, one by Ramarshi)
commentaries.gist: Notes that a similar idea occurs in the Dhammapada.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Compares Proverbs 17:12, that meeting a bear robbed of her cubs is better than meeting a fool in his folly.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi (1948 critical edition: textual status)
commentaries.gist: Ranked Group II (no. 320): in more than one manuscript version but not the secure core; absent from the southern recension.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to choosing environments: a modest job, flat or town with decent people can be better than a prestigious one among people who drag you down.
misreadings: Not contempt for tribal or rural people; the contrast is between hardship and bad company.
Not a licence to call anyone you dislike a fool and cut them off.
cautions: Can sound misanthropic; keep it about one's own choices of company.
speaks_to: weighing a prestigious but toxic workplace
choosing friends or a peer group
someone who left comfort for integrity
not_for: someone lonely or isolated who needs connection, not more distance
a reader in a family situation they cannot leave
research_note: Ramachandra Budhendra's text lacks this verse, so no traditional Sanskrit commentary was available for it beyond Pandey's modern one.

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 16 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.16; Kale and Wortham no. 16; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 12; Kosambi no. 15, Group I)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 15 confirmed (Group I). Addressed to kings (nṛpāḥ), as our setting says.
translation_note: Accurate. 'mānam ujjhata' is 'give up your pride'; Ramachandra Budhendra glosses māna as anger or stubbornness toward the learned, which fits the same sense.
context: In the section praising the learned, which opens with verses on poets living poor in a king's land. This verse tells rulers to drop their pride before people whose wealth is learning, because that wealth is beyond the reach of thieves, time and loss.

key_terms.sense: being given to those who ask; shared with seekers and students
the end of a cosmic age, the world's dissolution

core_teaching: Learning is a wealth that cannot be stolen, keeps giving joy, grows when shared and survives every loss; those who hold it deserve respect from the powerful.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Learning cannot be stolen; unlike money, whose earning brings pain, it yields indescribable happiness and grows by being taught. Kings should drop their anger toward the learned, since no one can rival them.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Addresses kings: before those who own this hidden, imperishable wealth that grows by giving, stop your arrogance; who can equal them?

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Kale's translation stresses that the 'secret wealth of knowledge' survives even the end of the world and increases when given to those who ask.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Explains kalpānta as the destruction at the end of a kalpa, a day of Brahma: learning outlasts even the world's dissolution.

practical_reading: A reminder that skills and understanding are the one asset no layoff, theft or market crash takes; and that teaching what you know enlarges it rather than spending it.
misreadings: Not a claim that learned people are above criticism; it is aimed at the arrogance of power.
Not a dismissal of material security.
cautions: Mentions the end of an age (kalpānta), a cosmic not personal image; harmless for most readers.
speaks_to: someone who lost money or a job but kept their skills
teachers and mentors
students doubting the worth of study
people facing condescension from the powerful
not_for: someone struggling to learn or excluded from education, who may feel shut out
a reader in financial crisis who needs practical help, not consolation

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 18 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.18; Kale and Wortham no. 18; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 14; Kosambi no. 38, Group I)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 38 confirmed (Group I).
translation_note: Accurate. Note 'vidhātā' is Brahma the creator; the line's 'Fate' is a fair modern gloss but commentators read Brahma, standing for an angry king.
context: In the praise of the learned, directly after verses telling kings not to slight scholars. The swan, famed for separating milk from water, stands for the scholar's discernment; the angry Creator stands for a king who can banish a scholar but not take his skill.

key_terms.sense: the Creator, Brahma; in the allegory, the angry ruler
sporting in a bed of lotuses: the swan's comforts

core_teaching: Circumstances, comforts and position can be taken away; a cultivated skill of discernment cannot.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as indirect speech (aprastuta-praśaṃsā): an angry king can only stop a scholar living in his realm, not take the skill his learning produced, so a king should not be angry with scholars.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Adds the explicit parallel: a king may seize a poet's wealth or bar him from court, but cannot snatch his poetic gift or learning; wherever such people go, they shine.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Quotes the scholiast: no one can take away the virtue of one whose good quality is part of his nature.

practical_reading: When you lose a role, a city or a comfortable setting, what you have cultivated in yourself travels with you; build skills that do not depend on one employer.
misreadings: Not a claim that losses do not hurt; the verse admits the swan really loses its lake.
Not a statement that fate is hostile; the 'angry creator' is a figure for an angry patron.
cautions: For someone who just lost a home or job, lead with the acknowledgment of loss before the consolation.
speaks_to: job loss or being pushed out of a position
relocation or exile from a familiar place
artists and scholars without patronage
not_for: fresh bereavement (the 'what remains' framing can feel dismissive)
someone whose skill itself was damaged by illness or injury

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 19 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.19; Kale and Wortham no. 19; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 15; Kosambi no. 76, Group I)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 76 (Group I). Our ref_label gives no Kosambi number.
translation_note: Accurate. 'saṃskṛtā' means speech refined (by grammar and culture, per Pandey and Ramachandra Budhendra), and 'dhāryate' held or maintained; 'refined and well held' is right. The line's 'well-chosen' is a fair simplification.
context: In the praise of learning, following verses on learning as unstealable wealth and the swan's discernment. It narrows the point to speech: cultivated speech is the ornament that lasts when jewellery and grooming fade.
core_teaching: External adornments fade; speech refined by learning and care is the one ornament that stays and truly makes a person attractive.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Goes through each adornment (armlets, pearl necklaces, bath, sandal and musk, jasmine, oiled hair) and says none adorns; refined speech alone does, as an ornament that never perishes.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: All ornaments are perishable; the beauty pure speech creates is lasting, so effort should go to the ornament of speech.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates 'saṃskṛtā' as speech 'possessed in a refined state' and the last clause as the one ornament that fades not.

practical_reading: Invest in how you speak: clarity, kindness and accuracy outlast looks and clothes, at interviews, in families and as we age.
misreadings: Not a sneer at grooming or dress; the comparison is about what lasts.
'Refined' does not mean elite Sanskrit or English; it means speech cultivated with care.
speaks_to: anxiety about appearance or ageing
preparing for interviews or public speaking
parents teaching children how to speak to others
not_for: someone with a speech or language disability, unless framed as care rather than polish

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 20 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.20; Kale and Wortham no. 20; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 16; Kosambi no. 70, Group I)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 70 confirmed (Group I).
translation_note: Accurate, including the final 'without learning a person is a beast', which our_note rightly says the line omits.
context: Part of the praise of learning, right after the verse on speech as the lasting ornament. It piles up titles for learning: beauty, hidden treasure, source of comfort and fame, teacher of teachers, kin abroad, highest deity, honoured by kings.

key_terms.sense: one without learning is a beast

core_teaching: Learning gives a person everything that beauty, money, family and status promise, and it goes with you everywhere, including far from home.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Learning is the beauty that shows without ornaments; teacher of teachers because it teaches the highest truth; kin abroad because it earns hospitality; highest deity because it can grant liberation; honoured in royal assemblies where wealth is not.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Learning is the best form, a secret treasure, giver of comfort and fame, revered even by elders, a companion abroad; one is honoured among kings for learning, not money; without it a person counts as a beast.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Renders 'gurūṇāṃ guruḥ' as 'the greatest benefactor' and keeps the closing line that one destitute of learning is a beast.

practical_reading: Speaks strongly to people building a life abroad: what you know becomes your network and your standing where you have no family.
misreadings: The closing 'a person without learning is a beast' is rhetorical; it must not be used to demean the unschooled.
Not a claim that degrees equal worth.
cautions: The final quarter is harsh; quote the verse selectively as our line does.
speaks_to: students and migrants starting out in a new country
someone who feels alone abroad
parents encouraging study
not_for: someone who could not study or left school early
readers with learning disabilities if the last quarter is quoted

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 21 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.21; Kale and Wortham no. 21; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 17; Kosambi no. 237, Group II)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 237: Group II, attested in several versions but listed among verses 'there is reason to suspect'. Our ref_label gives no Kosambi number.
translation_note: Our Sanskrit has a word-split error: 'विद्या न वन्द्या यदि' should be 'विद्याऽनवद्या यदि' (vidyā anavadyā, 'flawless learning'), as GRETIL, Kosambi and Ramachandra Budhendra read. As printed it would say 'if learning is not honoured'. The English 'spotless learning' is correct. 'jñāti' is kinsmen in the sense of rival co-heirs (dāyāda), per both commentators.
context: In the praise of learning, a chain of 'if you have X, what need of Y?' questions. Some items are virtues that make outward aids unnecessary (patience, a friend, learning, modesty, poetry); others are evils that are bad enough on their own (anger, rival kin, wicked people).

key_terms.sense: modesty, the sense of shame that recoils from wrongdoing

core_teaching: Inner qualities do the work of outer aids: patience protects better than armour and a true friend heals better than medicine; and inner faults like anger harm more than any outside enemy.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Forbearance blocks anger when insults come, so nothing can harm; anger is an inner enemy; rival heirs alone can burn up your wealth; a friend gives health; flawless learning secures every enjoyment; shame at wrongdoing is the ornament.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Summarises: forbearance is the greatest armour, anger the greatest enemy, co-heirs destroy like fire, a friend is the best medicine, the wicked are more venomous than snakes, faultless knowledge the best wealth.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Notes a variant 'vacanena' for 'kavacena' and reads 'anger, what need of enemies' as the inner passions being the worst foes.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates vrīḍā as 'a scrupulous conscience' and the kinsmen clause as kin doing the destructive work of fire.

practical_reading: Teachers take the first half as a checklist: cultivate patience instead of defences, notice that your own anger costs more than any rival, and value one true friend above remedies.
misreadings: The 'kinsmen are fire' clause is about inheritance rivalry, not a statement that family is bad.
Not a rejection of medicine or of wealth; it is a comparison of worth.
cautions: Contains a bitter line on kinsmen; avoid quoting it whole to someone in a family dispute or grieving a relative.
speaks_to: people who react with anger and want to change
someone grateful for a friend in illness
reflection on what really protects us
not_for: someone in an inheritance or family feud (the kinsmen clause will inflame)
a reader needing medical care who might hear 'no need of medicine'

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 23 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.23; Kale and Wortham no. 23; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 19; Kosambi no. 42, Group I)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 42 confirmed (Group I).
translation_note: Accurate. 'siñcati vāci satyam' (sprinkles truth into speech) is read by Telang and Wortham as 'makes one truthful in speech'.
context: In the praise of learning. Ramachandra Budhendra notes that, having praised the learned, the poet now states the benefit of good company (satsaṅgati). The verse lists what good company does and ends with a rhetorical question.

key_terms.sense: company of good and wise people
tell me! (a rhetorical address to the reader)

core_teaching: Spending time with good people improves almost everything about us: our thinking, our honesty, our standing and our peace of mind.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Good company removes dullness, makes one truthful, brings honour, removes sin through teaching dharma and clears the mind through teaching knowledge; so keep company with the good, not the wicked.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Company of the good takes away slowness of mind, brings truth into speech, raises respect, ends wrongdoing and spreads one's name; there is nothing it does not accomplish.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang (1874/1893 edition: notes citing two Sanskrit commentaries, one by Ramarshi)
commentaries.gist: Reads the phrase about truth in speech as making a person habitually truthful.

practical_reading: Choose friends, colleagues and mentors deliberately; the people around you shape your habits of mind and speech more than any resolution.
misreadings: Not a reason to look down on or shun people who are struggling; 'good company' means people of good character, not of high status.
speaks_to: choosing friends or a community
someone starting at a new college or job
parents thinking about a child's peer group
feeling stuck and needing new influences
not_for: someone isolated who cannot easily find such company (it may feel like blame)

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 25 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.25; Kale and Wortham no. 25; not in Ramachandra Budhendra's southern text; Kosambi no. 807, Group III)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 807 confirmed, but that puts it in Group III: stray verses found in single versions, isolated manuscripts or anthologies. It is in the common North Indian (Chaukhamba) text, so 'from the Nitishataka' is fine; do not present it as securely Bhartrihari's own.
translation_note: Mostly accurate. 'parijano avañcakaḥ' means household attendants or staff who do not cheat (Kale 'honest servants', Pandey 'trustworthy servant'), not 'kinsfolk'. 'satī priyatamā' is a chaste, beloved wife.
context: In the North Indian ordering it sits among the verses praising learning, just after a verse praising great poets. It is a list of the good things of a householder's life, ending with the claim that they come when Hari (Vishnu), who removes the world's troubles, is pleased.

key_terms.sense: a master or employer inclined to kindness
a mind without a trace of distress
a face made bright by learning

core_teaching: The blessings of an ordinary good life (family, work, friends, peace of mind, learning) are to be recognised as grace, not taken for granted.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Heads it 'the fruit of divine grace': only when Vishnu, protector of the worlds, is pleased does one gain a virtuous son, faithful wife, kind master, loving friend, trustworthy servant, untroubled mind, lasting wealth and learning.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates the attendants as 'honest servants' and the closing clause as these being obtained when Hari, who gratifies desires and pleases the world, is propitiated.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi (1948 critical edition: textual status)
commentaries.gist: Group III (no. 807): attested only in single versions or anthologies, with a different reading of the last line; the least secure class of verses ascribed to Bhartrihari.

practical_reading: Read as a gratitude list: name what is already good in your household, work and friendships, and treat it as gift rather than entitlement.
misreadings: Not a test of divine favour: lacking a child, spouse, kind boss or wealth does not mean God is displeased with you.
Not a prescription of gender roles; the Sanskrit names son and wife, but the point is gratitude for good relationships.
cautions: Implies that these blessings follow divine pleasure; for readers who are childless, widowed, single, unemployed or ill, it can read as a judgment.
speaks_to: gratitude practice
a settled householder counting blessings
someone recovering perspective after stress
not_for: infertility or child loss
divorce or widowhood
job loss or a harsh boss
chronic illness or depression (the 'mind at ease' line can sting)

context: A compact list of ethical restraints and virtues, called the path to the good that is common to all scriptures. In the North Indian order it closes the run of verses on learning and good company before the verse on three kinds of people (Niti 27).

key_terms.sense: giving at the right time, according to one's means
common to all the scriptures and traditions

core_teaching: Underneath differences of doctrine, every tradition agrees on a basic path: non-harm, honesty, not taking what is not yours, timely generosity, restraint of craving, humility and compassion.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Lists the virtues it names (non-violence, non-stealing, truthfulness, generosity, keeping out of talk about others' wives, freedom from greed, humility, kindness to all) as qualities that lead a person onto the path of welfare.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Renders the close as 'the way of happiness common in all the scriptures, that never fails in its operation'.

practical_reading: A short, interfaith ethical checklist for a day: harm no one, take nothing that is not yours, tell the truth, give what you can when it is needed, notice and interrupt craving, be kind.
misreadings: Not a claim that all religions are identical in doctrine; it says they agree on this ethical floor.
'Silence about others' wives' is about not gossiping or leering, not about women's speech.
cautions: The original includes a clause about not discussing other men's wives; if quoted whole, render it neutrally as not gossiping about others' partners.
speaks_to: someone wanting a simple moral compass
interfaith families or friendships
starting a fresh habit or vow
teaching children basic ethics
not_for: someone in scrupulosity or moral OCD who may turn the list into self-punishment

key_terms.sense: the low, the middling, the best
being struck back again and again

core_teaching: People differ less in talent than in how they meet obstacles: some never start, some stop when it gets hard, the best keep going through repeated setbacks.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: The low do not begin from fear of obstacles; the middling begin and are shaken off; the best, endowed with steadiness, finish despite repeated blows. Like the gods who churned on through poison until nectar appeared.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Calls it the difference between low, middling and high natures: the high-minded person completes what he starts without counting obstacles.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Notes the verse is quoted in the Mudrarakshasa, Act 2, and gives Wilson's verse translation of it there.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi (1948 critical edition: textual status)
commentaries.gist: Group II (no. 277): attested in several versions but among the verses Kosambi marks as open to suspicion.

practical_reading: Used to encourage finishing: expect obstacles as part of any real project, and judge yourself by whether you keep returning after setbacks, not by whether setbacks come.
misreadings: Not a judgment that people who hesitate are worthless; teachers use it to invite movement up the scale.

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 28 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.28; Kale and Wortham no. 28; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 56, in his section on the good; Kosambi no. 18, Group I)

translation_note: Accurate.
context: Closes the run of verses on the learned and the good in the North Indian order. It lists the hard code of good people and asks who taught them this 'sword's-edge vow'. A near-twin (Niti 64) ends with the same question.

key_terms.sense: do not ask favours of the wicked
an honest, just way of living or earning
stand tall, keep one's dignity in misfortune
a vow like walking on a sword's edge

core_teaching: Good people keep a demanding code even under pressure: they do not beg from the wicked or burden struggling friends, earn honestly, refuse what is base even at great cost, and keep their dignity in trouble.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: An honest livelihood is dear to them; nothing base, even at risk of life, rejecting the excuse that emergencies have no rules. Who taught them this vow? No one: it comes naturally to them.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Asks who set the good on this path, sharp as a sword's edge, where one cannot ask the wicked, cannot ask a poor friend for money, must keep an honest living and stay steady in trouble.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Following Telang, reads 'uccaiḥ stheyam' as retaining one's dignity in misfortune.

practical_reading: A guide for hard times: borrow from the right people or not at all, do not lean on a friend who is also struggling, keep earning honestly, and hold your head up while you get through it.
misreadings: Not a ban on asking for help; it rules out begging from the wicked and burdening the struggling.
'Even at the cost of life' is rhetorical intensity, not advice to risk one's life.

pressure to compromise at work
someone deciding whom to ask for help

someone already too proud to seek support
suicidal ideation

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 31 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.31; Kale and Wortham no. 31; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 23, in the section on honour and valour; Kosambi no. 57, Group I)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 57 confirmed (Group I). Wortham notes a parallel in the Hitopadesha (Suhrdbheda 40).
translation_note: Accurate. 'piṇḍada' is literally the one who gives the lump of food.
context: In the section on honour and spirit (mana-shaurya), after verses on the lion who will not eat what is beneath him. The dog and the elephant are two ways of depending on a patron: fawning, or steady self-respect.

key_terms.sense: the one who gives the food; patron, employer

core_teaching: Even when you depend on someone, you can keep your dignity; grovelling for favour is the mark of a small spirit.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: The dog shows its own lowness before the giver; the elephant looks on gravely and eats only after many coaxing words. These are the examples of the low and the high person.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Calls it the illustration of high and low: the small person, like a dog, shows grovelling humility to get fed; the great one stays dignified like the king of elephants and lives with self-respect.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the dog showing its mouth and belly and points to a parallel in the Hitopadesha.

practical_reading: At work or with patrons and donors, do your job well and be courteous without flattery; self-respect is compatible with depending on others.
misreadings: Not contempt for dogs or for anyone who must work for a living; it is about the posture of flattery.
Not a licence for arrogance or making others coax you; the elephant's quality is composure.
speaks_to: someone tempted to flatter a boss or client
people in service jobs keeping their dignity
job seekers and freelancers dealing with gatekeepers
not_for: someone who has had to plead to survive (it can shame them)
a reader in a coercive relationship

translation_note: Accurate. 'artha-ūṣman', the warmth or glow of wealth, is well kept.

key_terms.sense: the warmth or heat of wealth

core_teaching: Nothing about a person changes when they lose money, yet how they are seen and treated changes completely; the poet marvels at this.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Though senses, mind and speech stay as before, without wealth a person enters a strange state; the wonder is that when the warmth of money ends he seems in a moment a different man.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates: the same limbs, deeds, intellect and speech, yet without the warmth of wealth the man instantly becomes another being, and calls this strange.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi (1948 critical edition: textual status)
commentaries.gist: Group III (no. 512): found only in isolated versions or anthologies; reads 'the same deeds' rather than 'the same name'.

practical_reading: For someone who has lost income: the change you feel in others' eyes is about them and the world's habits, not about your worth or abilities.
misreadings: Not saying that money makes the person; the wonder is aimed at the world's judgement.
Not advice to chase wealth to be respected.
cautions: Can deepen shame if read as 'without money you are nobody'; frame the wonder as criticism of the world.

feeling treated differently after losing status
retirement and loss of a title
not_for: someone in acute financial crisis without support, unless paired with practical help
a reader already ashamed of poverty, if read flatly

core_teaching: Society credits the rich with every virtue: birth, learning, eloquence, looks. The verse states it as a law of the world.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: These days birth, learning, eloquence and looks are credited to whoever has money; a poor man with every virtue gets no respect. All virtues seem to live in gold.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates plainly: whoever has wealth is noble, learned, a sound critic, an orator and handsome; all virtues resort to wealth.

practical_reading: A clear-eyed observation to steady someone who feels overlooked: if people defer to the wealthy, that reflects social habit, not the real distribution of worth.
misreadings: Not advice that money is what makes a person good; our_note is right that read flat it inverts the point.

cautions: Easily misused as cynicism; pair with Niti 40 and 43.

noticing status bias at work or in marriage talks
young people under pressure to show off money
not_for: someone in financial distress who might hear 'without money you have no worth'

context: Ramachandra Budhendra says that with this and the next verse the poet shows how wealth and other goods are destroyed. It is a list of twelve causes of ruin, from a king's bad counsel to a person's careless spending.

key_terms.sense: affection is lost by living away (in another land)
friendship is lost through lack of warmth

core_teaching: Good things are rarely lost in one blow; they wear away through specific neglects: bad advice, attachment, spoiling, not studying, bad company, drink, inattention, distance, coldness, misconduct and carelessness.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Explains each cause: an ascetic falls by attachment (citing the Gita on desire born of attachment); a family is ruined by one bad son; affection for wife and children fades by living in other lands.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Draws the lessons: a king should take good counsel, an ascetic avoid attachment, a son not be over-pampered, the wise avoid bad company and drink, farming be watched, friendship tended, wealth guarded from unworthy recipients.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'saṅga' as attachment to objects of sense, since detachment is the ascetic's whole aim.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates the last clause as wealth dissipated by misdirected charity or careless expenditure.

practical_reading: A maintenance checklist for a life: friendships need warmth, relationships need presence, money needs attention, children need limits, and judgement needs good advisers.
misreadings: 'Affection is lost by living away' is an observation about neglect, not a verdict that migrants' families stop loving them.
Not an endorsement of harsh parenting; the tradition's maxim about beating children should not be carried over.
cautions: Ramachandra Budhendra supports 'spoiling ruins a son' with a maxim recommending beating over pampering; do not reproduce that in a modern reading.
The distance clause may sting readers living abroad or in long-distance relationships.

parents thinking about indulgence and limits
people managing money or a small business
leaders who rely on advisers
not_for: someone abroad who already feels guilty about distance from family
a parent grieving a child who went astray (the 'bad son ruins a family' clause)

attribution_note: Kosambi no. 50 confirmed (Group I).

context: In the section on wealth, following the list of ways good things are lost. It names the only three ways wealth can go and warns the hoarder.
core_teaching: Wealth will leave you one way or another: by giving, by using, or by loss. Whoever neither gives nor uses it chooses loss by default.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Wealth should be given and enjoyed, otherwise it is destroyed through theft and the like.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates the three as charity, enjoyment and destruction, the conditions to which wealth is subject.

practical_reading: Teachers use it against hoarding and anxious saving with no purpose: plan to give and to use what you have, or circumstances will decide for you.
misreadings: Not a case against saving for needs, emergencies or dependants; the target is the miser who neither gives nor uses.

someone deciding on charitable giving
families arguing over inheritance
people who never let themselves enjoy what they earn
not_for: someone who has just lost savings to fraud or disaster (it can sound like blame)

keeping gratitude after success
noticing entitlement in oneself
not_for: someone currently hungry or destitute, for whom it may sound like philosophising

business owners and employers
parents and teachers expecting results
community organisers

the pot, which draws only its own capacity

job seekers feeling desperate
comparing oneself to wealthier peers

someone repeatedly let down by promises
deciding whom to ask for help
not_for: someone who has run out of people to ask (it may feel like 'stop asking')
research_note: Absent from Ramachandra Budhendra's southern text, so no traditional Sanskrit commentary was available.

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 55 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.55; Kale and Wortham no. 55; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 44, end of his section on the wicked; Kosambi no. 37, Group I)
attribution_note: Our verified_with gives Kosambi no. 27; the stanza is Kosambi no. 37 (Group I, best-attested). Correct the citation.
translation_note: Fair, with variant readings in the fifth clause: GRETIL 'kiṃ guṇaiḥ' (what need of other virtues), Kosambi 'kiṃ janaiḥ' (what need of supporters), Ramachandra Budhendra 'kiṃ balena' (what need of a retinue). 'sumahimā' (GRETIL) vs 'svamahimā' (Kosambi). Our rendering follows GRETIL and is fine. Wortham reads the first two clauses as superlatives ('what vice can be worse').
context: Placed at the turn between the section on the wicked and the section on the good, it works as a hinge: a balance sheet of what makes all other faults or merits redundant. It follows the verse on honour and precedes the 'seven thorns in my mind' verse.

key_terms.sense: greed, wanting more; treated as the root fault
backbiting, carrying tales about others behind their backs
a clean mind, free of malice

core_teaching: One inner quality outweighs a pile of outward ones: greed and slander are enough to spoil a person, while truthfulness and a clean mind already do the work that penance and pilgrimage are meant to do.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Greed alone is enough blame; backbiting leads to ruin like the gravest sins; truth purifies more than fasts; a mind free of malice is the root of liberation, so pilgrimage adds nothing. Conclusion: work to acquire good qualities.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: A ranking: no flaw beyond greed, no sin above slander, no penance above truth; learning is the chief wealth and ill fame hurts worse than death. So drop greed and take up truth.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Links the last clause to the Roman ideal of preferring death to dishonour (Horace on Regulus), i.e. a classical honour-code sentiment.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Calls greed the greatest evil because most others spring from it; on goodness of heart, says courteous conduct wins over strangers, so such a person never lacks kin.

practical_reading: Use it as an audit: before adding rituals, good causes or possessions, check the one inner thing that would make them pointless (greed, gossip) or unnecessary (honesty, a clean mind).
misreadings: Not a dismissal of pilgrimage or practice as such; the verse ranks inner purity above them.
The last clause ('if disgrace, what need of death') is rhetoric about honour, never a suggestion that a disgraced person is better dead.
cautions: Last clause equates disgrace with death; avoid for anyone facing public shame, scandal, exam failure or job loss, and never quote it alone. Our misuse line already flags this; keep it.
speaks_to: someone tempted to buy their way to virtue with rituals or donations
a person trying to stop gossiping
someone wanting a simple inner checklist
not_for: anyone living through public humiliation or with suicidal thoughts
someone being shamed by their community

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 57 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.57, reading 'vahati' for 'dahati'; Kale and Wortham no. 57; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 46, section on the wicked; Kosambi no. 60, Group I)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 60 confirmed (Group I).
translation_note: Accurate. 'hotāram' is the priest or sacrificer pouring the oblation (Kale: any sacrificer; Pandey: the hotṛ priest). 'Fire burns even the hand that feeds it' in our line is a fair compression.
context: In the section on the wicked, among verses about the dangers of court life. It is followed directly by the famous verse on how hard service to a master is (silent servants are called dumb, talkative ones forward).

key_terms.sense: one's own person, someone truly close
the priest in the very act of offering

core_teaching: A person ruled by fierce anger has no one truly close: like fire, they hurt even those who serve and feed them.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: No one counts as their own for violently angry kings; even someone who serves them well will be burned, as fire burns the sacrificer who touches it. Therefore such a king should not be served.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Everyone fears a hot-tempered ruler, so none is his own; heads it 'the harm of anger' and draws the lesson that a ruler should not be fierce in temper.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as no one being a favourite of fiercely angry kings, with fire burning the sacrificer who touches it; takes the sacrificer in a general sense.

practical_reading: Two directions: if you have a temper, notice that it pushes away the very people who look after you; if you work or live near someone like that, it names why loyalty does not make you safe.
misreadings: Not a reason to stay close to a volatile person in the hope that devotion will protect you.
Not a claim that the people who get burned deserved it.
cautions: Can describe an abusive household or boss; for a reader in that situation, pair it with practical safety and support, not acceptance.
speaks_to: someone whose temper is costing them relationships
employees of a volatile boss
a leader reflecting on how their anger lands
not_for: someone being told to tolerate an abusive partner or parent

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 60 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.60; Kale and Wortham no. 60; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 49, section on the wicked; Kosambi no. 62, Group I)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 62 confirmed (Group I).
translation_note: Accurate. The image is the shadow (chāyā) of the forenoon, long at first and shrinking towards noon, versus the afternoon shadow, short at first and lengthening. Our line's 'like afternoon shade' fits. Wortham turns it into morning and midday light, which loses the shadow image.
context: Near the end of the section on the wicked: having described the wicked, the poet contrasts their friendship with the friendship of the good, just before the next verse on deer, fish and the good being harassed by hunters, fishermen and slanderers for no reason.

key_terms.sense: the first and second halves of the day

core_teaching: Judge a friendship by its direction, not its start: the false kind opens big and shrinks, the true kind starts small and keeps growing.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Forenoon shadow is long and shrinks; afternoon shadow is short and grows. So the friendship of the wicked begins large and wanes, that of the good begins slight and increases; a sensible person should act on this.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Explains the two shadows the same way and draws the plain rule: make friends with the good, not with the wicked.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Calls it a clever picture of friendship as found in the world: insincere friendship is most demonstrative at the start, good friendship hardly visible at first but steadily increasing.

practical_reading: Be slow to trust intense early warmth, and patient with quiet friendships that seem modest now; watch which way each one is moving over months.
misreadings: Not a claim that every friendship that starts warmly is false.
Not a reason to write off a friend after one cold patch.
speaks_to: someone hurt by a friendship that burned bright and faded
a new arrival in a city or job making friends
someone doubting a slow, steady friendship
not_for: someone isolated and lonely who might hear it as 'distrust anyone friendly'

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 62 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.62; Kale and Wortham no. 62; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 51, opening his section on the good; Kosambi no. 43, Group I)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 43 confirmed (Group I). Kosambi's last words read 'tebhyo 'parebhyo namaḥ'; GRETIL 'tebhyo narebhyo namaḥ'.
translation_note: Accurate on the usual reading. One clause is read two ways: 'śaktir ātma-damane' is the strength to master oneself (Kale, Pandey: control of the mind), but Ramachandra Budhendra takes it as the power to respond when one is humiliated, i.e. not passive meekness. 'svayoṣiti ratiḥ' is love for one's own wife.
context: Opens the section on the good (sujana-paddhati) in both the northern and the southern ordering, right after the verses on the wicked. It is a salutation to people who carry a list of qualities.

key_terms.sense: delight in other people's good qualities
an addiction, a passion, for learning
strength in self-mastery (one commentator: strength when humiliated)
staying free of the company of the wicked

core_teaching: Goodness is a cluster of everyday habits (seeking good company, enjoying others' merits, humility before teachers, love of learning, faithfulness, devotion, self-mastery) and the people who carry them deserve honour.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Each quality is set against its opposite: longing for the company of the wise (a door to liberation, citing Yoga Vasishtha), joy in others' merits rather than fault-finding, humility to the teacher, faithfulness, devotion to Shiva as the supreme deity.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'strength in ātma-damana' as prowess when oneself is slighted, not indifference, quoting a saying that forbearance is the usual ornament but valour suits the moment of insult.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the self-mastery clause as power to restrain the mind; those who hold these qualities are truly great, to be saluted and imitated.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates it as a bow to people in whom the listed sterling qualities reside, including devotion to the trident-holder (Shiva) and strength to restrain the self.

practical_reading: Pick one item from the list (enjoying someone else's success, seeking better company, studying) and practise it this week; notice the people around you who already live it and honour them.
misreadings: Not a sectarian test; the devotion clause names Shiva, but the list is broadly ethical.
Self-mastery here is not self-suppression or swallowing mistreatment.
cautions: Includes 'love for one's own wife' and devotion to Shiva; render inclusively (faithfulness to one's partner) if used for a general reader.
speaks_to: someone choosing role models or mentors
a student wanting a character checklist
someone trying to stop envying others
not_for: someone using lists of virtues to judge themselves harshly

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 63 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.63; Kale and Wortham no. 63; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 52, section on the good; Kosambi no. 14, Group I). Wortham notes it is also in the Hitopadesha (Mitralabha).
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 14 confirmed (Group I). Also quoted in the Hitopadesha per Wortham, so it circulated as a common subhashita.
translation_note: Accurate. 'kṣamā' in success is forbearance or patience (Kale 'forgiveness'); readings vary between 'abhiruci' and 'abhirati' (love of fame), same sense. 'śrutau vyasanam' is a passion for scripture or learning (Kale: the Vedas).
context: Second verse of the section on the good: after saluting good people, the poet lists the qualities that come to the great-souled by nature, each matched to its proper occasion.

key_terms.sense: forbearance at the height of success
skill in speech in an assembly
natural, established by one's own nature

core_teaching: Greatness shows as the right quality at the right time: steadiness when things go wrong, patience when they go right, clear speech among people, courage in a real fight, love of learning.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Pairs each quality with what it excludes: steadiness without dejection in trouble, patience without arrogance in prosperity, eloquence rather than silence in a learned court, valour rather than flight; all native to the great.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Gives word meanings and stresses that these are inborn characteristics of the great-souled, not traits put on for show.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates the qualities and notes that the frequent mention of Vedic study in these poems suggests Bhartrihari was not a Buddhist.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Notes it also appears in the Hitopadesha and that the variant words for 'love of fame' carry the same sense.

practical_reading: Ask which situation you are in today, setback or success, and practise the matching virtue: steadiness for the first, restraint and patience for the second.
misreadings: 'Natural to the great' is not a claim that ordinary people cannot learn these qualities.
Courage 'in battle' is about rising to a real contest, not a licence for aggression.
speaks_to: someone in a setback looking for steadiness
someone newly successful or promoted
students and young professionals building character
not_for: someone in acute crisis who may hear 'the great are naturally steady' as a judgement on their distress

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 64 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.64; Kale and Wortham no. 64; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 57, section on the good; Kosambi no. 275, Group II)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 275 confirmed, but that is Group II (authenticity open to doubt). It is in the common northern text and in Ramachandra Budhendra's southern text, so 'from the Nitishataka' is fine.
translation_note: Accurate. 'sambhrama-vidhiḥ' is the eager bustle of honouring a guest (Telang via Kale; Wortham 'cheerful hospitality'). GRETIL reads 'anabhibhava-gandhāḥ' (without a whiff of contempt); Kosambi 'nirabhibhava-sārāḥ', same sense.
context: In the section on the good. Its refrain 'who taught the good this sword's-edge vow?' echoes an earlier verse (Niti 28, the first asidhara-vrata), making this the second list of hard, quiet disciplines of good people.

key_terms.sense: silence after doing someone a kindness
speaking in public of help one has received
a vow as hard as walking a sword's edge

core_teaching: Real goodness is a set of quiet asymmetries: hide your own kindnesses, announce others' kindness to you, welcome people warmly, stay humble when rich, and speak of others without contempt.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Secret giving bears greater fruit; rise to greet a visitor; after a favour stay silent (citing Manu, do not proclaim a gift); speak publicly of favours received, or you become ungrateful; talk of others without censure.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Calls it a very hard rule of the good: giving without publicising, honouring guests, never mentioning one's own help but telling everyone of others', no pride in prosperity, never speaking scornfully of anyone.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Notes the sword-edge vow was proverbial for an extremely hard discipline (also explained as continence beside a young wife) and that the verse is quoted in the Kuvalayananda.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Explains 'upakṛti' as favours received from others, set against the kindness one has done oneself, and the sword-edge vow as a proverb for a near-impossible task.

practical_reading: Do one kind thing today and tell no one; publicly thank someone who helped you; notice whether your talk about absent people carries a hint of contempt.
misreadings: Not a ban on ever acknowledging one's own work (for instance, at a job review).
Secret giving is not secrecy about money from a spouse or family.
speaks_to: someone who wants recognition for their help
donors and volunteers
a newly wealthy person
someone who wants to stop gossiping
not_for: someone whose unpaid work is already invisible and unthanked (carers, homemakers); it may sound like 'stay invisible'

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 66 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.66; Kale and Wortham no. 66; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 55, section on the good; Kosambi no. 335, Group II)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 335 (Group II, authenticity doubtful); our record cited no Kosambi number. Present in both northern and southern texts.
translation_note: Accurate. Our own note is right: the verse describes the great; our line turns it into a command ('be soft... be firm'). Acceptable as a reading, but the card should not present the imperative as the poet's words.
context: A short couplet in the section on the good, on how the minds of the great respond to fortune and misfortune; it follows the verse on the natural ornaments of the great.

key_terms.sense: hard as a mass of rock from a great mountain
in times of plenty / in times of trouble

core_teaching: The great are gentle and generous when things go well, and unbreakably firm when things go badly; the usual human pattern (hard in success, soft in trouble) is reversed.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: In prosperity their heart turns tender, never hard; in disaster it becomes hard as a rock pile, meaning their steadiness does not loosen. He quotes a verse describing the good as unshaken in danger and not puffed up in wealth.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: In good times the great are compassionate; in adversity they bear it with a heart hard like mountain rock.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Compares Proverbs on the righteous as an everlasting foundation and Horace's just man whom nothing shakes.

practical_reading: When things are good, let it make you kinder and more giving; when things are hard, let it make you firmer, not harder on others.
misreadings: Hardness in adversity is firmness of resolve, not coldness towards people or suppressing grief.
cautions: 'Be hard as rock in adversity' can be heard as 'don't feel'; for grief or distress, frame it as steadiness, not emotional shutdown.
speaks_to: someone in a tough stretch who needs to hold steady
someone newly comfortable who wants to stay kind
leaders
not_for: someone in fresh grief who needs permission to be soft

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 67 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.67; Kale and Wortham no. 67; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 58, section on the good, with a different last line; Kosambi no. 33, Group I)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 33 (Group I, best-attested); our record cited no Kosambi number. Kosambi ends 'saṃvāsato jāyate' (comes from living together) where GRETIL has 'saṃsargato'.
translation_note: Accurate. 'svātyām' is under the Svati star (the folk belief that rain falling into an oyster when the moon is in Svati becomes a pearl). Ramachandra Budhendra's text ends differently ('such are the ways of the low, middling and best'), turning the last line into a statement about three kinds of people rather than about company.
context: In the section on the good, on how surroundings shape character. Three fates of one drop of water illustrate the low, middling and high results of association.

key_terms.sense: an oyster under the Svati star
from association, the company one keeps

core_teaching: The same drop vanishes, sparkles or becomes a pearl depending on where it lands; as a rule, people too become low, middling or excellent according to their company.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: On hot iron not even the water's name survives; on a lotus leaf it looks like a pearl without being one; in the oyster it becomes one. His text applies this to low, middling and best people.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: As a rule, low company makes one low and ruins one, middling company middling, best company best: this is the power of association.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Reads the three as an ascending scale of dispositions: one that leaves no result, one pleasing to look at, and one both beautiful and valuable.

practical_reading: Look at where you spend your hours and with whom; move a little of that time toward people and places that bring out your best.
misreadings: Not a licence to look down on people as 'hot iron'.
'Prāyeṇa' (as a rule) is a hedge: company shapes but does not wholly determine a person.
cautions: Can read as blaming people stuck in harsh environments; frame as encouragement to seek good company, not judgement of anyone's origins.
speaks_to: a student or young adult choosing friends
someone leaving a toxic workplace or group
parents thinking about a child's company
not_for: someone who cannot leave their environment (it may feel like a verdict)

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 68 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.68; Kale and Wortham no. 68; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 59, section on the good; Kosambi no. 279, Group II)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 279 confirmed: Group II (authenticity doubtful).
translation_note: Accurate. 'samakriyam' means acting the same, i.e. behaving alike in trouble and in good times.
context: In the section on the good: defines three relationships by their conduct rather than their title, and calls finding all three a reward of past merit. The following verse in the southern text and the friend-marks verse (Niti 73) take up the friend again.

key_terms.sense: the same in trouble and in happiness
those who have done good, the meritorious

core_teaching: A son, a wife or a friend is defined by how they act, not by the label; the real thing in each is rare and counted as a blessing earned by goodness.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: A son is one who pleases his father by obedience and good conduct, not merely one born; a wife one devoted to her husband's welfare; a friend one alike in trouble and prosperity. Only the meritorious gain all three.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: A virtuous son, a wife who seeks her husband's good and a friend with equal sympathy in joy and sorrow are obtained only through great merit.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates the three definitions plainly and the close as only the meritorious securing this triad.

practical_reading: Our card uses only the friend line: be the friend who shows up the same way in someone's bad week as in their good one.
misreadings: Not a judgement that people without a good child, spouse or friend lack merit.
The wife clause is one-sided; do not use it to prescribe roles.
cautions: Ties having good family and friends to past merit; for someone estranged, widowed, childless or friendless it can sound like blame. Our record already restricts the card to the friend line; keep that.
speaks_to: someone reflecting on what a real friend is
gratitude for a steady friend
not_for: someone estranged from family or in a difficult marriage
someone grieving a child or spouse

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 70 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.70; Kale and Wortham no. 69; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 60, closing his section on the good; Kosambi no. 36, Group I)
attribution_note: Our verified_with gives Kosambi no. 26; the stanza is Kosambi no. 36 (Group I). Kale/Wortham number it 69 because their text lacks GRETIL 1.69.
translation_note: Accurate. 'dūṣayantaḥ' (GRETIL, Kosambi): shaming or showing up the slanderers; Ramachandra Budhendra reads 'duḥkhayantaḥ' (pain them). Wortham misreads the clause as the good 'hating the evil speaker'; Kale and Pandey match our rendering.
context: Closes the section on the good with a summary portrait built on paradoxes: rising by bowing, praising oneself by praising others, serving oneself by serving others, defeating slanderers by patience.
core_teaching: The good win by apparent reversals: humility lifts them, praising others reveals their own worth, working for others gets their own work done, and patience leaves slanderers exposed.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Humility itself is the cause of their rise; they reveal their virtues by praising others, never by self-praise; they achieve their ends by putting others' work first; they pain harsh speakers by forbearance alone, not by fierceness.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the third line as making the harsh-mouthed wicked ashamed by forgiveness alone; the good, of wondrous conduct, are honoured by all.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates the third clause as censuring calumniators, whose mouths are noisy with harsh words of accusation, with their patience alone.

practical_reading: Next time you are criticised unfairly, try answering with calm and good work rather than a counter-attack; next time you want credit, give some away first.
misreadings: Patience with slander is not silence about abuse or harassment (our misuse line says this; keep it).
Not a strategy of fake humility to get ahead.
cautions: For someone being bullied or harassed, 'answer with patience' must not become 'put up with it'.
speaks_to: someone facing gossip or unfair criticism at work
someone tempted to self-promote
leaders
not_for: a victim of harassment or abuse

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 71 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.71; Kale and Wortham no. 70; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 61, opening his section on helping others; Kosambi no. 63, Group I). The same stanza occurs in Kalidasa's Abhijnanashakuntalam per Wortham and Telang.
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 63 (Group I); our record cited no Kosambi number. Caution: the identical stanza is in Kalidasa's Shakuntala, so authorship is shared or borrowed; say 'also in Kalidasa's Shakuntala' if attributing.
translation_note: Accurate. Kosambi reads 'bhūri-vilambinaḥ' (hang very low) for 'dūra-vilambinaḥ'; Ramachandra Budhendra notes a variant 'anarthitāḥ' (the good help unasked).
context: Opens the section on helping others (paropakara-paddhati). Three natural images of fullness that bows down rather than puffing up.

key_terms.sense: bowed down by their load of fruit
the very nature of those who help others

core_teaching: Real abundance bends toward others: as fruit-laden trees and rain-heavy clouds hang low, the good become humbler as they prosper, because what they have is for giving.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Trees bow under fruit; clouds hang low to rain everywhere; the good, though prosperous, are not fierce. This is natural to benefactors, who do not count effort for others as hardship; quotes 'trees bear fruit for others'.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Trees, clouds and good men bend because their fruit, water and wealth exist for others, not themselves; humility is the innate dharma of those who help.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Notes the stanza also occurs in Kalidasa's Shakuntala with a minor variant ('āgamaiḥ' for 'udgamaiḥ').

practical_reading: Measure success by how much lower it lets you bend toward others: more patience, more listening, more sharing.
misreadings: Not an argument that the poor or struggling are less humble or less good.
speaks_to: someone newly successful or promoted
people in leadership
someone who admires quiet, generous people

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 72 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.72; Kale and Wortham no. 71; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 62, section on helping others; Kosambi no. 54, Group I)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 54 confirmed (Group I).
translation_note: Mostly accurate. 'śruta' is what has been heard, i.e. sacred learning or scripture heard from a teacher (Kale 'Vedic knowledge', Ramachandra Budhendra 'hearing the dharma texts'), not just 'listening' as our line says. 'Ears shine by listening' is loose; 'by what they have learned' is closer.
context: In the section on helping others, right after the verse on the humility of benefactors; it lists the true ornaments of a compassionate person. It echoes an earlier verse (Niti 65) on the ornaments of the great.
core_teaching: Each part of the body is truly adorned by its right use (the ear by learning, the hand by giving, the whole body by serving others), not by jewellery or perfume.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: The ear shines by hearing dharma teaching, not gold earrings; the hand by giving to the worthy, not a golden bracelet; the body by doing good, not musk-sandal paste. These natural ornaments last; jewellery perishes.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Learning, giving and service produce a lasting beauty in ear, hand and body that perishable earrings, bracelets and sandal paste cannot; so these are what the good collect.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Cross-refers to the earlier ornament verse and to the New Testament on inner rather than outward adornment.

practical_reading: Before dressing up for an occasion, ask what your hands, ears and time will actually do there: learn something, give something, help someone.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of jewellery or self-care; it ranks them below use.
speaks_to: someone caught up in appearance or status
teenagers and young adults
a wedding or festival season reflection

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 73 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.73; Kale and Wortham no. 72; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 65, section on helping others; Kosambi no. 31, Group I)

key_terms.sense: does not abandon you in trouble

core_teaching: A true friend is known by six acts: checking your wrongs, steering you to good, keeping your secrets, speaking up for your strengths, staying in your trouble, and giving in time of need.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Turns you from sin by advice on dharma, urges you to good deeds, hides your secrets, proclaims your virtues, stays even in deep trouble, gives what is needed in calamity; cross-refers to Niti 68.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: A good friend stops harmful acts, sets you to beneficial ones, hides what should be hidden, publicises your merits, stays in adversity and supplies help when needed.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as the wise describing the marks of a true friend, including helping you in time of need.

practical_reading: Use it both ways: test one friendship against the six marks, and pick one mark to practise for a friend this week, such as telling someone else what you admire about them.
misreadings: Keeping secrets does not mean covering up harm or abuse; the first mark is stopping wrongdoing.
speaks_to: someone wondering if a friendship is real
someone who wants to be a better friend
a friend in a crisis
not_for: someone recently betrayed by a friend may find it painful; pair with gentleness
