context: In the section on helping others, a four-way classification of people by how they treat others' interests. The punchline is the last class, who destroy others' good for no gain at all.

key_terms.sense: those who bring about others' good
without conflict with their own interest
who they are, we do not know (no name is bad enough)

core_teaching: People range from those who give up their own interest for others, to those who help when it costs them nothing, to those who harm others for gain, to those who harm others for no reason at all, the last being worse than any name.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Ranks them as best, middling, demon-like and a fourth group so far outside the three that they cannot be classed, the very lowest; advice: join the best class you can.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Gives the four grades in order (some good people, ordinary people, human-demons, and those we cannot even name) with word-by-word meanings.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates the first class as the noblest, the second as men of the middle order, the third as demons in human form; we know not what to call the fourth.

practical_reading: An honest mirror: most of us live in the 'ordinary' band; the verse invites one step up, and a hard look at any harm we do out of spite or habit with nothing to gain.
misreadings: Not a licence to label people demons.
Being 'ordinary' (helping without self-harm) is not condemned.
cautions: Harsh language ('demons in human form'); for someone recently hurt by another person it can feed rage or rumination.
speaks_to: someone reflecting on their motives for helping
someone puzzled by pointless cruelty or trolling
team or community ethics discussions
not_for: someone consumed by anger at a specific person

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 76 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.76; Kale and Wortham no. 75; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 66, section on helping others; Kosambi no. 28, Group I)
attribution_note: Kosambi no. 28 confirmed (Group I).
translation_note: Accurate and matches Kale, Pandey and Ramachandra Budhendra: water evaporates when the milk is heated, the milk boils up to follow, and settles when water is added. Wortham reads the sequence differently (water boils over first, milk follows, together they quench the fire); our version is the commentators' reading.
context: In the section on helping others: a small kitchen parable explaining the friendship of the good, right after the four kinds of people and the marks of a true friend.
core_teaching: Good friends give each other what they have, cannot bear to see each other suffer, and are calmed only by being together again.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Milk gave water its sweetness and whiteness; water, unable to bear the milk's heating, sacrificed itself; milk rose to follow it into the fire and settled only when water was added. True friends cannot bear each other's pain.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Water, remembering the milk's gift of its qualities, burns itself away; milk then tries to leap into the fire and calms only when water is added. Good friends share qualities, bear hardship, and are healed by reunion.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Calls it a fine moral drawn from a kitchen fact: well-heated milk boils over, and adding water settles it.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as friends acting together against a common enemy, at the cost of their own lives, and cites a Hitopadesha line on water quenching fire.

practical_reading: Notice who has given you something of themselves; when they are under strain, show up, and when you are boiling over, let a friend's presence settle you.
misreadings: Not a call to self-destruction for a friend; the image is mutual care, not martyrdom.
cautions: The image of 'offering itself into fire' can be heard as self-sacrifice; avoid for someone in a codependent or self-erasing relationship.
speaks_to: someone grateful for a close friend
someone missing a friend who has moved away
reconciliation after distance
not_for: someone in a codependent relationship
someone grieving a friend's death (the reunion image may sting)

attribution_note: Kosambi no. 44 confirmed (Group I).
translation_note: Accurate for the GRETIL/Budhendra reading 'prakhyāpaya praśrayam' (show courtesy, humility toward elders). Kosambi, Kale and Wortham read 'pracchādaya svān guṇān' (conceal your own virtues) instead; Kosambi also has 'pāpe matim' for 'ratim'. Mention the variant if a writer wants 'hide your virtues'.
context: Near the end of the section on helping others: a run of twelve imperatives summing up the conduct of the good, before the verse asking how many such people there really are.

key_terms.sense: kill arrogance (pride of learning or status)
conciliate even those hostile to you
be kind to whoever is suffering

core_teaching: Goodness is a daily practice of small decisions: let go of craving and pride, forgive, tell the truth, learn from the wise, respect those who deserve it, reach out even to opponents, guard your name, and be kind to anyone in pain.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Gives each command a reason: cut craving with dispassion or hope's ropes bind you; forgive insults or temper wrecks your work; win over enemies, citing the Gita's evenness to foe and friend, or they exploit your weak spots.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'praśraya' as humility toward teachers and elders, to be made visible, and 'guard your good name' as making one's birth worthwhile.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Lists these as the very form of good conduct and human duty; renders the enemy clause as keeping even enemies content.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates with the variant 'do not parade your good qualities' and discusses the grammar of the imperatives.

practical_reading: Choose one of the twelve for today (for example, one kind act for someone suffering, or one conciliatory message to someone you are at odds with).
misreadings: Winning over an enemy is not tolerating harm (our misuse line; keep it).
'Guard your good name' is not image management at the cost of honesty.
cautions: Forbearance and conciliation should not be pressed on someone in an abusive situation.
speaks_to: someone wanting a daily practice list
someone in a long-running conflict
someone struggling with craving or ambition
not_for: a victim of abuse being urged to 'win over' the abuser

attribution_note: Kosambi no. 19 confirmed (Group I). Our verified_with also cites Vivekananda's Complete Works; not verified in this pass.
translation_note: Accurate. 'kiyantaḥ' is a rhetorical 'how many?', i.e. very few (Ramachandra Budhendra, Pandey, Wortham).
context: Closes the section on helping others in the southern text. A portrait of the rare good person, ending in the question 'how many are there?'.

key_terms.sense: full of the nectar of goodness
making mountains of the atoms of others' virtues
blossoming, glad in their own hearts

core_teaching: The rarest goodness is consistent in thought, word and deed, and magnifies the smallest good in others while rejoicing inwardly at it; such people are few.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Devoted to good acts with all three instruments (mind, speech, body); they enlarge even others' tiny virtues and are glad at heart; 'how many' means few, since such qualities are uncommon.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Such people, full of the nectar of good deeds and delighted by others' small merits, can be counted on one's fingers.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Reads the question as expecting the answer 'but few', comparing the Gita's 'among thousands, scarcely one strives for perfection'.

practical_reading: Turn the usual habit around: today, make a mountain out of someone's small good deed (say it aloud, thank them) and a molehill of their small fault.
misreadings: Not a claim that good people do not exist; it says they are rare and precious.
speaks_to: someone who tends to criticise
managers and parents
someone wanting to appreciate others more

attribution_note: Kosambi no. 21 confirmed (Group I).
translation_note: Translation accurate, but our Sanskrit has a typo: 'कण्ठाधारी' (kaṇṭhādhārī) should be 'कन्थाधारी' (kanthādhārī, wearing a patched rag-quilt), as in GRETIL, Kosambi and Ramachandra Budhendra. Our 'wears rags' already follows the correct word.
context: In the section on steadfastness (dhairya-paddhati), right after the verse on the gods who kept churning the ocean despite jewels and poison until they got the nectar. It portrays the person of spirit who is indifferent to comfort while pursuing a goal.

key_terms.sense: sleeping on the ground / on a couch
living on greens / enjoying fine rice
a person of spirit, set on the task

core_teaching: Someone fully committed to a purpose stops keeping score of comfort and discomfort; floor or bed, plain or fine food, rags or silk, all are equal next to the work.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Whether on hard ground or a soft couch, plain greens or rich food, rags or golden robes, the high-minded seeker of a goal counts neither pain nor pleasure but stays even while pursuing the work.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: A person bent on accomplishing a task with a firm mind sleeps on thorny ground or a soft bed as place and time require and takes whatever food or clothing comes; only the goal matters.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Compares Gita 2.15: the steady person unmoved by these contacts, the same in pain and pleasure, is fit for immortality.

practical_reading: In a demanding season (exams, a start-up, caring for someone), let go of comparing your comforts with what you had or what others have; keep your eye on the purpose.
misreadings: Not a glorification of neglecting sleep, food or health.
Not a reason to impose hardship on others who did not choose the goal.
cautions: Can feed hustle culture; for someone near burnout, pair with rest (see Niti 86 misuse line).
speaks_to: students in exam season
founders and people in demanding projects
someone adjusting to a drop in lifestyle
not_for: someone burnt out or neglecting health
someone in poverty not by choice (it may romanticise hardship)

translation_note: Accurate. 'jñānasyopaśamaḥ' is calm or tranquillity as the ornament of knowledge; 'nirvyājatā' is freedom from pretence. 'śīlam' is character, good conduct. Our_note's 'forgiveness belongs to the one able to do otherwise' matches 'prabhavituḥ' (one who has power).
context: Closes the section on steadfastness in the southern text; in the northern order it sits among the steadfastness verses. It pairs eight strengths with the quality that makes each beautiful, then crowns character as the ornament of all.

key_terms.sense: courtesy, as the ornament of power
restraint of speech, as the ornament of valour
forgiveness, as the ornament of one with power

core_teaching: Every strength has a matching restraint that makes it admirable (power with courtesy, courage with few words, learning with humility, wealth with wise giving, authority with forgiveness), and character underlies them all.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Contrasts each ornament with its spoiling opposite: courtesy not wickedness in lordship, measured speech not rambling in a hero, humility not arrogance in learning, giving to the worthy not to flatterers in wealth; character outranks them all.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Glosses each pair word by word: courtesy adorns prosperity, measured use of speech adorns valour, calm adorns knowledge, humility adorns learning, using wealth for a worthy recipient adorns money.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates restraint over the senses as the ornament of learning and good character as 'the root of all' and the ornament of all things.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Renders the last line as natural disposition, parent of the virtues in each, being the highest ornament.

practical_reading: Name your main strength (skill, money, authority, knowledge) and practise its matching restraint today: the expert listens, the boss forgives, the strong one speaks less.
misreadings: 'Forgiveness adorns the powerful' does not ask the powerless to forgive abuse.
speaks_to: new managers and people with authority
high achievers
students and young professionals

verified_ref: Bhartrihari, Nitishataka 84 (GRETIL/Chaukhamba 1.84; Kale and Wortham no. 83; Ramachandra Budhendra no. 74, section on steadfastness; Kosambi no. 265, Group II)

context: In the section on steadfastness, after the verses on the person of spirit indifferent to comfort. It names the four great pressures (opinion, fortune, life, time) and says none moves the steadfast off the just path.

key_terms.sense: let death come this very day
from the path of what is right

core_teaching: The steadfast do not let praise or blame, gain or loss, or even the timing of death decide their conduct; they hold to what is right.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Whether the shrewd blame or praise, wealth comes or freely goes, death comes now or in another age, the steadfast do not move a single footstep from the just path; that path, not opinion, is their highest aim.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: The firm-minded do not care for blame or praise, whether wealth is gained or not, or even death; they never stray from the just path and do only what is just.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates the steadfast ('persons of mental calibre') as not swerving from the path of justice whatever politicians say or wealth does.

practical_reading: Before a hard decision, set aside what people will say and what it will cost you, and ask only what is right; then take one step on that path.
misreadings: Not stubbornness: 'the right path' is justice, not one's own opinion.
Not contempt for feedback.
cautions: Mentions death ('let death come today'); fine as resolve, but avoid for a reader with suicidal thoughts or fresh bereavement.
speaks_to: whistle-blowers and people under pressure to cut corners
someone facing criticism for a principled choice
someone tempted by money to compromise
not_for: someone in fresh grief or with thoughts of death
someone being rigid who needs to hear others

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi (1948 critical edition: textual status)

athletes and students
encouragement after a fall
not_for: chronic illness or disability
long or complicated grief
someone in a prolonged crisis

key_terms.sense: a great enemy that lives inside your own body
does not sink, does not come to grief

core_teaching: The worst enemy is the inertia inside us, and the best friend is steady effort; one who keeps working does not go under.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: External enemies spoil one's work, but sloth is an enemy inside the body, so how could success come? Effort helps like a kinsman, since one who works can hope for results; so abandon sloth and stay industrious.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi (1948 critical edition: textual status)
commentaries.gist: Group II, no. 216 (doubtful authenticity), reading 'having made which one does not sink'.

practical_reading: When stuck, do the smallest next action rather than waiting to feel ready; effort, even small, is the friend that gets you moving.
misreadings: Rest is not laziness; burnout needs rest, not more effort (our misuse line; keep it).

students before exams
someone restarting after a long pause
not_for: someone depressed or burnt out
someone with chronic illness or fatigue
